title: Build your own header library (sort.h + sort.c)
learningGoals: split code into a header (declarations) and a source file (definitions)
include your own header with quotes
protect a header with an include guard and explain what the preprocessor does with it
compile and link several .c files with one gcc command

youtube.title: Make Your Own #include: sort.h From Scratch | C EP 82
youtube.description: printf comes from stdio.h. Today you write your own header. We move our sorts into sort.h and sort.c, add a stats struct that counts comparisons and swaps, and learn the include guard that stops a header from being pasted twice. Plus the exact GCC errors you get without one. 0:00 Make your own #include · 0:20 Title · 0:25 .h vs .c · 1:10 Code: sort.h · 2:00 Code: sort.c · 2:50 Code: report.h and main.c · 3:35 Compile and link · 4:05 Pun · 4:10 What #include really does · 4:50 Bug of the Day · 6:20 Challenge · 6:45 Outro

scenes.narration: Since Episode 4 you've written hash include stdio dot h, and printf just worked. Someone wrote that header for you. Today, you write your own. By the end of this episode, any program you write can say hash include "sort.h" and get all your sorts for free.

scenes.onScreen: EP 82 · BUILD YOUR OWN HEADER LIBRARY
scenes.narration: Episode 82. Build your own header library.

scenes.onScreen: Restaurant menu (sort.h: what's available) vs kitchen (sort.c: how it's made); main.c is the customer
scenes.animation: Menu card flips; kitchen door swings
scenes.narration: Think of a restaurant. The menu tells you what you can order: names and prices, no recipes. That's the header file, sort.h. It lists the functions that exist, their names, parameters and return types. The kitchen is where the food is actually made. That's sort.c, the function bodies. And main.c is the customer: it reads the menu and orders. You split files like this in Episode 36. Today we turn it into a proper reusable library.

[HL 1] hash ifndef SORT_H: if SORT_H is not defined yet, keep reading. [HL 2] hash define SORT_H: define it now. These two lines, plus the hash endif at the bottom, are the include guard. We'll see why they matter in a minute. [HL 4] A struct from Module 9, SortStats, with two counters, [HL 5] comparisons [HL 6] and swaps. [HL 7] typedef, from Episode 63, lets us just write SortStats. [HL 9] Then the prototypes: print_array, [HL 10] bubble_sort and [HL 11] insertion_sort. Each sort now takes a pointer to a SortStats so it can report its work. No function bodies here, just the menu. [HL 13] hash endif closes the guard.

scenes.onScreen: sort.c (42 lines), zoomed on lines 1–2 and 10–26
scenes.narration: [HL 1] sort.c needs printf, so it includes stdio.h. [HL 2] And it includes our own header, with double quotes instead of angle brackets. Quotes mean: look in my project folder first. Including your own header in its .c file lets GCC check that the bodies match the prototypes. [HL 10] bubble_sort is our version from Episode 74, with stats added. [HL 14] Every comparison, we do stats arrow comparisons plus plus. [TRACK stats->comparisons=1] The arrow is for accessing a struct through a pointer, from Episode 62. [HL 19] Every swap, stats arrow swaps plus plus. [TRACK stats->swaps=1] Insertion sort, further down, counts the same way, with each shift counted as a swap.

scenes.onScreen: report.h (8 lines), report.c (6 lines), main.c (17 lines) side by side
scenes.animation: [HL] cues; arrows show main.c including both headers and report.h including sort.h
scenes.narration: We also make a tiny second library, report. [HL report.h 4] report.h includes sort.h, because print_stats needs the SortStats type. [HL report.c 4] report.c prints a name and the two counters. [HL main.c 2] main.c includes sort.h, [HL main.c 3] and report.h. Notice: sort.h now arrives twice, once directly and once through report.h. Hold that thought. [HL main.c 8] Each sort gets its own stats, starting at zero, [HL main.c 10] and we pass their addresses.

scenes.onScreen: `gcc main.c sort.c report.c -o sorter` and 3 output lines
scenes.animation: Three .c files fly into gcc, one .exe comes out
scenes.narration: To build, list every .c file: gcc main.c sort.c report.c minus o sorter. GCC compiles each file separately, then the linker joins them into one program. You never put .h files in the gcc command; they're pasted in by hash include. Run it: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9. Bubble: 14 comparisons, 8 swaps. Insertion: 11 comparisons, 8 shifts. The same numbers as our step traces in Episodes 74 and 76.
Why did the header file never get invited back? It kept including itself.

scenes.onScreen: Preprocessor view of main.c: sort.h pasted once, report.h pasted, then sort.h again but skipped because SORT_H is defined
scenes.animation: Pasted blocks slide in; second sort.h block hits a butter "SORT_H already defined" gate and bounces off
scenes.narration: Here's the secret: hash include is copy-paste. Before compiling, the preprocessor replaces the line with the whole header file. So in main.c, sort.h is pasted. Then report.h is pasted, and inside it, sort.h tries to come in a second time. But now SORT_H is already defined, so hash ifndef SORT_H is false, and the preprocessor skips straight to the hash endif. Nothing is pasted twice. That's the include guard doing its job.

scenes.animation: Red siren; second sort.h paste collides with the first, sparks
scenes.narration: Today's bug: missing include guards. Delete the three guard lines from sort.h and build again. GCC stops with errors. Conflicting types for SortStats, previous declaration of SortStats. Then conflicting types for bubble_sort and insertion_sort. Why conflicting, when they're identical? Because each time the typedef is pasted, it creates a brand-new struct type with no name of its own, and two different struct types can't share the name SortStats. The functions then conflict because their parameter types now point at two different structs. The fix: always wrap every header in ifndef, define, endif, with a name made from the file name in capitals.

Your challenge: make search.h and search.c with linear_search and binary_search from Episode 73, with their own include guard. Then write a main that sorts an array with your library and finds 6 with binary_search.
Next episode, the last in this module: two data structures you use every day without noticing, stacks and queues. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.fixed: Fixed: wrap sort.h in `#ifndef SORT_H` / `#define SORT_H` … `#endif` (as in Code shown).
bug.why: main.c pulls sort.h in twice (directly and via report.h), and each paste of the anonymous typedef struct creates a new, different type named SortStats; the guard makes the second paste empty.

pun: Why did the header file never get invited back? It kept including itself.
challenge: Create search.h and search.c with linear_search and binary_search (from EP 73) and an include guard named SEARCH_H. In main, sort {5, 2, 9, 1, 6, 3} with insertion_sort from your library, then find 6 with binary_search.

shorts.title: Make your own #include
shorts.hook: "stdio.h was written by someone. Write yours."
shorts.script: Every C program starts with hash include stdio dot h. Someone wrote that file. Today you write your own: sort dot h. Then any program can include it and get your sorting functions for free.
shorts.caption: Your own C library in 7 minutes.

shorts.title: .h vs .c in 30 seconds
shorts.script: A header file is the menu: function names and parameters, no bodies. The .c file is the kitchen: the actual code. Hash include is just copy-paste of the menu into your file. And the include guard, ifndef, define, endif, makes sure the menu is pasted only once, even if two files ask for it.
shorts.caption: Header files finally explained.

shorts.title: Conflicting types for SortStats
shorts.script: main.c includes sort.h, and so does report.h. Without an include guard, sort.h gets pasted twice. Each paste of the typedef struct makes a new type, so GCC says conflicting types for SortStats. Add ifndef SORT_H, define SORT_H, and endif. Every header, every time.
shorts.caption: Three lines that save your build.

shorts.title: Kept including itself
shorts.script: Why did the header file never get invited back? It kept including itself.
shorts.caption: Know your guards.

shorts.title: Build search.h
shorts.script: Make search dot h and search dot c with linear and binary search, with their own include guard. Sort an array with your library, then find 6 with binary search. Post your gcc command in the comments.
shorts.caption: Grow your own C library.
